findings: F1 rho support: the mechanism text says 'mid-rank empirical-CDF rank rho_i in (0,1)' and the computation 'cohesion mid-rank rho' says 'rho in (0,1]^{n_train}', but the formula ( #{j: coh_j<coh_i} + 0.5*#{j: coh_j=coh_i, j<i} ) / (n_train-1) attains 0 for the least cohesive item (no j below it, no ties before it) and 1 for the most cohesive item. Both stated ranges are wrong and they contradict each other; the support must be stated as rho_i in [0,1] (the deg_i=0 default 0.5 lying in the interior).

F2 self-neighbour: the computation 'adjacency counts A' explicitly allows A_ii>0 ('unless (i,i) occurs adjacently'), but 'top-D neighbourhood' defines N(i) as the D indices j with the largest A_ij without excluding j=i, while the idea says 'neighbours'. If i in N(i) then sim_ii = |N(i)|/deg_i enters coh_i and shifts every rho. The specification must state N(i) subset of {j != i} (or explicitly include i and then restate sim_ii and the coh bound), because the cached rho depends on it.

F3 isolated items in the mid-rank: coh_i is undefined for deg_i=0 and a separate computation overwrites rho_i = 0.5 afterwards, yet the mid-rank counts #{j: coh_j<coh_i}, #{j: coh_j=coh_i} run over all j and the denominator is fixed at n_train-1. Whether deg_i=0 items enter the counts, and whether the denominator is n_train-1 or (#deg>0)-1, is not stated and changes every rho value; and once a point mass at 0.5 is written in, the note 'uniform marginal' is false. The specification must fix the ranking population and its denominator (rank only deg_i>0 items over (#deg>0 - 1) and then overwrite the rest, or include them as a 0.5 tie block) and drop the uniform-marginal claim.

F4 degree note: the note on the computation 'degree' says deg is 'used both as the top-D key tie-breaker denominator and in sim_ij and coh_i'. The top-D key is A_ij and ties are broken by ascending item id, never by deg. deg is used only in D = ceil(mean deg), in sim_ij and in coh_i (and as the zero-degree test); the note must say that.

F5 training integration: training_integration.loss says 'the baseline's objective plus the mechanism's contribution', which contradicts the computation 'Stage-2 objective' ('adds NO auxiliary term, no regulariser on rho, no penalty on the offset'; the coupling lives entirely inside C). The loss must be stated as exactly the baseline's L_rec, with the behaviour signal entering only through C -> P. The idea's Stage-2 integration (epochs 0..2999, batch 1023, baseline seed, frozen SID table exported for Stage 3) is also missing from training_integration.

F6 gradient rules incomplete: gradient_rules contains only 'the continuous surface' (autograd through the statements) and 'the argmin of the assignment' (no gradient). It never states (a) that a_k receives gradient only through P -> C -> |rho_i - s_k|, nor what happens if the baseline detaches P (the idea's 'documented fallback' is not 'mechanism unchanged': a_k then never leaves its quantile init and the strata degenerate to fixed quantiles), (b) that rho_i and the frozen beta carry no gradient, (c) that q_k receives both the reconstruction gradient on the chosen raw row q_{k1} and the STE cost-path gradient through d_c, while u_i receives only the STE path dL/dp -> dL/dP -> C -> d_c. These paths must be stated explicitly in the specification, not left in the idea's equations block.

rho range is stated twice and both statements are mathematically wrong: the mechanism text says 'rho_i in (0,1)' and the 'cohesion mid-rank rho' output says 'rho in (0,1]^{n_train}', but rho_i = (#{j: coh_j < coh_i} + 0.5*#{j: coh_j = coh_i, j < i})/(n_train-1) equals 0 for the unique minimum-cohesion item and 1 for the maximum, so the achievable range is [0,1]; both strings must be replaced by that one correct range.

the mid-rank counts are not defined over items with undefined cohesion: #{j: coh_j < coh_i} and #{j: coh_j = coh_i, j < i} range over all j, yet coh_j is explicitly 'left undefined' when deg_j = 0 and only rho_i is later overwritten with 0.5. The spec never says whether deg_j = 0 items are excluded from the counts (in which case the stated denominator n_train-1 is wrong, because rho would top out at (n_train-1-n_iso)/(n_train-1)) or are given a finite coh value. Every rho, and therefore the whole behaviour offset, depends on this choice; it must be stated explicitly in the 'cohesion mid-rank rho' definition.

the 'cohesion mid-rank rho' note claims 'uniform marginal'. That is false: mid-ranks with ties plus the hard overwrite rho_i = 0.5 for every deg_i = 0 item concentrate mass at 0.5, and if deg=0 items are kept in the counts the denominator no longer matches the number of ranked items. The claim must be removed or replaced by 'empirical mid-rank in [0,1]; uniform only if no item is isolated and no ties' — nothing in the idea asserts uniformity.

the gradient path to a_k is hedged instead of stated: gradient_rules says 'a_k: only through P -> C -> |rho_i - s_k| ...; if the baseline detaches P, a_k stays at its quantile init (documented fallback, mechanism unchanged)'. This contradicts the spec's own straight-through note ('backward it is the identity on P_i, i.e. dL/dP = dL/dp, the baseline's STE, unchanged', so P is not detached) and the idea's claim that the reconstruction gradient reaches a_k through the plan. The spec must assert unconditionally that the Sinkhorn is unrolled and dL/dP flows into C and hence into a_k, and drop the detach fallback; otherwise the learned strata may never train and the described mechanism is not the one specified.

training_integration.loss states 'the baseline's objective plus the mechanism's contribution', which asserts an additive term, while the 'Stage-2 objective' computation states that the mechanism adds NO auxiliary term, no regulariser and no commitment loss of its own and that the behaviour signal enters only through C. The loss field must state that L is exactly the baseline Stage-2 objective, with no additive contribution.

Gradient path severed at the level-1 reconstruction: the computation 'level-1 reconstruction and residual' and the 'outputs' list define e1_i = q_{k1_i} as a hard index gather, while k1 = argmax_k P_ik carries no gradient. With that definition the straight-through selector p_i = one_hot(k1_i) + P_i - stop_grad(P_i) is produced and then never used downstream, so the reconstruction loss reaches neither a_k (the only trainable new parameter) nor the encoder through P -> C -> d_c; the a.grad test in the 'behaviour offset' note and the claim 'dL/dP = dL/dp' in the 'straight-through selector' note cannot hold. It must instead read e1_i = sum_k p_ik q_k (raw q_k, never y_k; forward value equals q_{k1_i}, backward gives dL/dP_ik = <dL/de1_i, q_k>), which is what the idea's STE and gradient_rules state.

Sign error in the stated offset gradient: the 'behaviour offset' note gives dO/da_k = -beta*R_c*s_k*(1-s_k)*sign(rho_i - s_k). With O_ik = beta*(1-|rho_i - s_k|)*R_c and s_k = sigmoid(a_k), d/ds_k (1 - |rho_i - s_k|) = +sign(rho_i - s_k), hence dO/da_k = +beta*R_c*s_k*(1-s_k)*sign(rho_i - s_k). The leading minus inverts the direction that should move a_k toward the item's cohesion rank (and, once C = d_c - O is differentiated, double-flips it). The formula must be stated with the plus sign, or the sign convention of C = d_c - O restated so that the two agree.

rho normalisation/population changed: the spec defines rho_i = (b_i + 0.5 t_i)/(n_pos - 1) with both counts over S = {i : deg_i > 0} and declares the range [0,1]; the idea fixes rho_i = (#{j: coh(j)<coh(i)} + 0.5*#{j: coh(j)=coh(i), j<i})/(n_train - 1) with n_train = 24556 and states rho in (0,1) with 0.5 for isolated items. Must be restored to the denominator n_train - 1 and the population of the idea (isolated items excluded from the counts, included in the denominator via the 24556 normaliser); with that denominator the achievable range is [0, (n_pos-1)/(n_train-1)], not the closed [0,1] the spec claims, and the note ordering the reviewer to reject any '(0,1)' string imposes on the idea a formula the idea does not have.

wrong sign in the stated offset gradient: the spec writes dO/da_k = -beta*R_c*s_k*(1-s_k)*sign(rho_i - s_k). With O_ik = beta*(1-|rho_i - s_k|)*R_c and s_k = sigmoid(a_k) the derivative is dO/da_k = +beta*R_c*s_k*(1-s_k)*sign(rho_i - s_k); the minus sign belongs to dC/da_k = -dO/da_k. The spec must state the sign correctly (autograd will anyway produce the correct path, but as written the documented gradient contradicts the formula).

gradient path stated unconditionally and the idea's fallback dropped: the idea declares the a_k path as 'only through P -> C -> |rho_i - s_k|; if the baseline detaches P, a_k stays at its quantile init (documented fallback, mechanism unchanged)'. The spec instead asserts 'Unrolled, not detached ... back-propagates through Ktilde into C' and adds a test that P.grad_fn is not None. The baseline's Sinkhorn is unchanged and the mechanism cannot guarantee it is unrolled, so the conditional must be kept and the unconditional assertion (and its test) removed; otherwise the specification promises a gradient to a_k that may not exist.

Cohesion rank (computations['cohesion rank']): the definition uses rho_i = (b_i + t_i/2)/n_train with t_i counted '(i included)', a full midrank. The idea's formula is rho_i = (#{j: coh_j < coh_i} + 0.5*#{j: coh_j = coh_i, j < i})/(n_train - 1), i.e. the tie term counts only j < i, so tied items get DIFFERENT rho in the idea and identical rho in the spec. The deviation is presented as a change of the denominator only; the tie rule is changed silently. The definition must either keep the idea's 0.5*#{j < i} tie term or state explicitly that the tie rule is also changed and give the tied items' common value.

Cohesion rank, stated reason for the denominator: the spec says the idea's n_train-1 'puts the unique maximum at (n_train - 0.5)/(n_train - 1) > 1'. That is arithmetically false for the idea's formula: with the j<i tie term the unique maximum has b_i = n_train-1 and no tie contribution, so rho = (n_train-1)/(n_train-1) = 1 exactly, and the unique minimum is 0 exactly. The correct justification is that the idea's normalisation attains 0 and 1, hence is not in (0,1); the false inequality must be replaced (and the same 1.0 endpoint also shows the idea's own range claim fails, which the spec must say).

Cohesion statistic (computations['cohesion statistic']): coh_i = (1/deg_i)*sum_{j in N(i)} sim_ij divides by deg_i, which is 0 for any item with no training edge (0/0), yet the output is claimed to be 'coh_i in [0,1] for every training item'. The isolated case must be defined in the cohesion statistic itself (explicit value, or exclusion from the counts), not left to the rank step.

Cohesion rank, no-edge items: the definition feeds no-edge items into b_i and t_i with 'coh = the value the idea assigns it (0.5)'. The idea assigns rho_i = 0.5 to such items, never a cohesion value; assigning them coh = 0.5 shifts b_i by the number of isolated items for every item with coh > 0.5, and it clashes with the same items' rho being overwritten to 0.5. The fill value for a missing coh must be declared as a specification choice with its consequence on the edged items' ranks, and not attributed to the idea.

The idea requires the baseline's Sinkhorn to keep 'same row sums 1 and column sums B/K' (B = 1023, K1 = 256), but the spec defines the plan only as P = Sinkhorn(center(C), sk_epsilon, sk_iters), and no marginal (row sum 1, column sum B/K) appears anywhere in the specification. The column marginal fixes the scaling v and therefore changes the relative values of P across codewords, hence the argmax k1, so this is not cosmetic: the definition must state P = diag(u) Ktilde diag(v) with Ktilde = exp(-center(C)/sk_epsilon), row sums 1 and column sums B/K, exactly as the baseline and the idea do, and must not leave the marginals implicit.

SWITCH BEHAVIOUR_OFF (switches[0]): the arm itself is right (offset zeroed) but its stated justification is false about the mechanism. It says 'the offset is k-independent in that arm (it is the same at every codeword), and a k-independent offset cannot change the argmax', whereas the mechanism's offset O_ik = beta*R_c*(1 - |rho_i - s_k|) is k-DEPENDENT through s_k, and that k-dependence is the entire reason the stratum can change the plan and the argmax. Only the zeroed offset is k-independent, so as written the justification contradicts the mechanism it is meant to justify (read literally it says the offset cannot change the assignment, i.e. the mechanism is a no-op). It must read: the arm sets O_ik = 0 for every k, removing the k-dependent s_k term, so C_ik = D_k and the assignment is the plain hyperbolic-cost balanced one, which is what makes the arm behaviour-free.

training_integration.optimizer: alpha_k is declared the mechanism's only trainable parameter ('the TRAINABLE code stratum', 256 scalars) and the spec asserts the reconstruction gradient trains it through P, yet the optimiser statement is 'the baseline's, unchanged; no new parameter group' and nothing anywhere says alpha_k is registered with (or added to a group of) the baseline optimiser. computations -> 'cohesion rank' (definition): the midrank is divided by |P| - 1 and the counts are restricted to P, and the text calls this 'the one repair the specification declares'. The idea fixes rho_i = (#{j: coh(j) < coh(i)} + 0.5*#{j: coh(j) = coh(i), j < i}) / (n_train - 1) over the training items, with the no-edge items set to 0.5. Whenever |P| < n_train this changes every rho_i, hence every C_ik, the plan P and k1 - i.e. the mechanism itself, not a clarification. It must use the idea's n_train - 1 denominator over the fixed training item set; if the compressed support really breaks the offset, that is an amendment to the idea and must be returned there, not written into the specification.

computations -> 'cohesion rank' (output 'rho_i in [0,1]' and the closing 'puts the ranked items exactly on [0,1]') contradicts mechanism ('rho_i in (0,1)') and the idea's range. With the midrank the minimum item gets rho = 0 (under both denominators) and, with the |P| - 1 denominator, the maximum gets rho = 1, while the strata s_k = sigmoid(alpha_k) live in the open (0,1): rho = 0 can never be matched by any s_k and the offset beta*R_c*(1 - |rho_i - s_k|) never reaches its maximum at the bottom of the ordering. The specification must state one support - the idea's (0,1) - and use a convention whose realised values stay strictly inside it (e.g. the midpoint (midrank + 0.5)/n, or the idea's own n_train - 1 denominator with the zero endpoint removed), not assert both (0,1) and [0,1].

level-1 STE and the alpha_k gradient path are contradictory. mechanism says 'the residual recursion, the reconstruction and the straight-through estimator are the baseline's, unchanged', while 'level-1 reconstruction and residual' declares 'DECLARED DEVIATION: the framework's canonical conventions describe the baseline's straight-through estimator x_q = x + (x_q - x).detach()' and uses p_i = one_hot(k1_i) + P_i - stop_grad(P_i); gradient_rules -> alpha_k then makes the gradient 'unconditional'. The idea makes it conditional ('if the baseline detaches P, a_k stays at its quantile init (documented fallback, mechanism unchanged)'), and the specification's own 'straight_through' convention names the detaching estimator as the baseline's. It must name one estimator: either the baseline's plan estimator is p_i = one_hot + P - stop_grad(P) (and then it is not a deviation), or the canonical baseline estimator holds and the idea's frozen-alpha fallback must be carried as the rule; an unconditional 'alpha_k is trained' cannot rest on both.

The rank population and the one-pass cache are never fixed. Nothing in the specification says rho is computed ONCE, before Stage 2, on the training split, over exactly the 24556 Stage-2 training items, and cached as float32 [24556] and looked up by item id: 'n_train' is used in the rank denominator but is never tied to that item set, the cohesion input is only 'the training split's user sequences (history -> target)', D, deg_i and the rank carry no population statement, and rho appears only as a 'frozen buffer' of the batch. The size of n_train and hence of |P| - 1 (or n_train - 1) depends on it, so it must be stated explicitly, with the dtype and shape of the cache.

cohesion rank (computations['cohesion rank']): the midrank counts are restricted to P = {deg>0} and divided by (|P|-1) ('rho_i = ( ... ) / (|P| - 1)', and 'Dividing by |P| - 1 instead ...'). The idea -- and the spec's own 'IDEA SPEC EQUATIONS' block in the same document -- give rho_i = ( #{j: coh_j < coh_i} + 0.5*#{j: coh_j = coh_i, j < i} ) / (n_train - 1) over the n_train = 24556 Stage-2 training items. As written the document carries two incompatible formulas for rho_i, and the numbers fed into C_ik = D_k - beta*R_c*(1-|rho_i - s_k|) are not the idea's. The definition must state the idea's n_train - 1 denominator (and, if the support [0, (|P|-1)/(n_train-1)] is judged a real scale mismatch with s_k, that must be raised as an amendment of the idea and approved, not folded into the definition as an unapproved repair).

conventions.straight_through: the conventions block states 'the reconstruction gradient reaches the encoder through the straight-through estimator x_q = x + (x_q - x).detach()'. That estimator detaches the plan, so P carries no gradient, |rho_i - s_k| receives none and alpha_k stays at its logit((k+0.5)/K) initialisation - exactly the fallback the idea documents and this spec explicitly disowns. It directly contradicts the level-1 reconstruction computation and the gradient rule 'alpha_k: TRAINED, and the rule is unconditional'. The conventions entry must be rewritten to the plan estimator p_i = one_hot(k1_i) + P_i - stop_grad(P_i) with P kept in the differentiable path (and to say the encoder gradient arrives through dP/dC, not as an identity), otherwise two mutually exclusive gradient paths are specified and an implementer following 'conventions' freezes the mechanism's only new parameter.

cohesion statistic (scale/normalisation): coh_i = (1/deg_i) * sum_{j in N(i)} sim_ij divides by the FULL degree deg_i while the sum runs only over the truncated neighbourhood N(i), |N(i)| = min(D, deg_i) <= deg_i. For every item with deg_i > D (about half of them, since D = ceil(mean degree)) coh_i is capped at D/deg_i < 1, so the claimed common [0,1] scale is never reached and coh - hence the rank rho_i that is built on it - partly ranks DEGREE rather than neighbourhood closure. It must be coh_i = (1/|N(i)|) * sum_{j in N(i)} sim_ij with |N(i)| = min(D, deg_i), or the spec must state the attained range [0, min(D,deg_i)/deg_i] and that coh_i is not comparable across items of different degree.

cohesion rank range: the mechanism text says 'a bounded cohesion rank rho_i in (0,1)', but the rank computation divides a count that is 0 for the unique minimum-cohesion item by |P| - 1 and the computation itself concludes '[0,1]'; the strict interval (0,1) is therefore unattainable and contradicts the same specification's own formula. The mechanism text must say rho_i in [0,1] (0 for the minimum ranked item, 1 for the maximum), consistent with the 'cohesion rank' computation and with the idea's amended equation.

cohesion statistic output: the output field says 'coh_i in [0,1] for every training item i', but the definition states that coh_i is DEFINED only for deg_i > 0 and that an item with no training edge has no neighbourhood, no sim and no cohesion. The output must be 'coh_i in [0,1] for the items with at least one training edge; undefined (and not computed) for the isolated items, which take rho_i = 0.5'.

cost matrix / beta: beta is defined as 'median over the items of the first batch of D_{i,k1(i)}' while training uses 1023 items per rank, so it is unspecified whether the median runs over the global first batch or over one rank's local batch. Since beta is measured once and frozen, a per-rank median would freeze a different scalar on each rank and make the cost matrix, and therefore the plan and k1, rank-dependent. The spec must state that the median is taken over the global first batch (synchronised across ranks) and the identical scalar is broadcast and frozen on every rank.

mechanism summary: it states 'the ONE thing the mechanism changes at level 1 is the estimator', but the same paragraph and the 'cost matrix' computation change the level-1 cost to C_ik = d_c(x_i,y_k) - beta*R_c*(1-|rho_i - s_k|), which is the mechanism. The summary must list the level-1 COST (geodesic distance minus the behaviour offset, fed to the baseline's balanced Sinkhorn) together with the plan-estimator as the two things the mechanism changes at level 1; only the estimator is a deviation from the baseline, the cost is the mechanism itself.

conventions.straight_through still states the canonical estimator x_q = x + (x_q - x).detach(), which carries no gradient through the plan and therefore freezes alpha_k, while the computation 'level-1 reconstruction and residual' and the gradient_rules make p_i = one_hot(k1_i) + P_i - stop_grad(P_i) the normative estimator; the contract field must be replaced by the plan estimator (and must say that with this estimator the encoder's reconstruction gradient flows only through dP/dC, because the identity term x is absent).

Scale mismatch at the endpoints: 'cohesion rank' declares rho to span the closed [0,1] ('the smallest item's mid-rank is 0, so the range is [0,1] ... the same scale as the strata') while s_k = sigmoid(alpha_k) is strictly inside (0,1). The extreme-ranked items therefore can never reach |rho_i - s_k| = 0 and are systematically penalised; rho and s_k must be put on one and the same open interval (e.g. rho_i = (rank_i + 0.5)/|P|, or clip rho to [0.5/|P|, 1 - 0.5/|P|]).

The justification 'Dividing by |P| - 1 puts the ranked items exactly on [0,1]' is false under the specification's own one-sided tie term 0.5*#{j in P : coh_j = coh_i and j < i}: with g items tied at the maximum cohesion the largest rank is |P| - 1 - 0.5*(g-1) < |P| - 1, so the top of the ordering never reaches the top stratum. Either use the symmetric mid-rank and state that ties bunch the ranks below the top, or drop the 'fill [0,1]' claim and justify the normaliser differently.

Notation collision on the codeword: 'dimensions' gives q as a bare 'K1 x D' and the executable sets q = lift(a, c), i.e. q is the LIFTED codebook exp_0^c(a), whereas the idea's q_k is the RAW codeword that reconstruction and the residual recursion use (a_{k1}, never y_k). The reconstruction is only correct because the executable happens to use a, not q. The keys must be renamed and labelled (a raw codeword, y_k = exp_0^c(a) lifted), with q_i renamed as the reconstruction, so that the raw/lifted distinction cannot be mis-implemented.

The rho buffer is specified only as 'a frozen buffer': its dtype, its length and its index alignment are never stated, although the idea requires float32 [24556] cached once over the Stage-2 training items and Stage 2 gathers rho_i by the global item id of each batch row, and the k1 table is exported per item. The specification must state float32, the buffer length (one entry per Stage-2 training item, 24556) and that the batch entries are gathered by item id.

The 'cohesion rank' computation divides by (|P| - 1), but the idea's formula is rho_i = (...) / (n_train - 1). This changes every edge item's rho by the factor (n_train-1)/(|P|-1), and it changes the idea's stated range from (0,1) to [0,1]. It must use n_train-1 exactly as the idea states and report the induced range [0, (|P|-1)/(n_train-1)] for edge items (0.5 for edge-less items), or the idea text must be explicitly amended before this specification can claim it.

In 'cost matrix', beta is defined as the median over only the 1023 items of the FIRST BATCH of RANK 0 and then broadcast. The idea says median over the batch. The justification that the ranks' latents agree at step 0 is false: identical parameters do not make different data batches have the same median, so rank 0's median is not the batch median. It must measure the median over the actual batch (all items on all ranks) or explicitly define and synchronize the per-rank batch; it cannot substitute rank 0.

In 'cohesion statistic', the definition keeps coh_i = (1/deg_i) sum_{j in N(i)} sim_ij but claims that using the rank of coh means the scaling cannot dominate. That is false: rank is invariant only under monotone transformations, and 1/deg_i is item-dependent, so it changes the ordering and confounds cohesion with degree. It must either normalize by |N(i)| = min(D, deg_i) (an average overlap) or use the raw sum and state the degree confound; the claim must be removed.

In 'geometry', the inputs are r and a, but the definition never states u_i = r_i, q_k = a_k, x_i = LIFT(u_i), y_k = LIFT(q_k), or D_ik = DIST(x_i, y_k). It also uses a for the raw codebook and q for the lifted codebook, while the idea reserves q_k for the raw codewords and y_k for the lifted codewords. D_k is therefore undefined and ambiguous. It must use the idea's symbols and state the mappings explicitly.

The GEOMETRY_OFF switch says c=0 keeps R_c=1 and that the two arms differ ONLY in the distance, but beta = m/R_c uses m measured from d_c; at c=0 that median is a Euclidean median, so beta changes, or if the curved beta is reused, the offset scale is not matched to the Euclidean distance. The switch must state whether m is re-measured at c=0 or the c=1 beta is frozen, and it must not claim the arms differ only in the distance unless that choice is made consistent.

The idea fixes the graph over the 24556 Stage-2 training items and caches rho as float32[24556]; the specification nowhere states 24556, the item universe, or the float32 cache. It only says 'the training split' and dimensions rho_i: B, so the population that defines the degree, P, |P|-1 and the frozen buffer is undefined. It must state the 24556-item universe and the float32[24556] frozen buffer.

The 'cohesion rank' calls rho a mid-rank, but the tie term only counts tied items with j < i; tied items therefore receive different ranks. A true midrank ties them at 0.5*(#{<}+#{=}). It must either implement the true midrank or call the statistic a tie-broken rank, not a midrank.

The continuous_surface declares a curvature argument with scalar 0.25, but its executable statements hardcode c = 1.0 and never read that argument; calling distance(x,y,0.25) still evaluates c=1. STAGE 2 - deviations found.
1) "cohesion statistic" definition uses coh_i = (1/|N(i)|)*sum_{j in N(i)} sim_ij; |N(i)| = min(deg_i, D), so every item with deg_i > D is inflated by deg_i/D. The idea says coh(i) = (1/deg_i)*sum_{j in N(i)} sim_ij.
2) "cohesion rank" uses (b_i + t_i/2 + 0.5)/n_pos over P only, with a symmetric average over ties; the idea says (#{coh_j<coh_i} + 0.5*#{coh_j=coh_i, j<i})/(n_train-1) over the train items. Both the denominator (scale of |rho_i - s_k| against the uniform quantile strata) and the tie convention are changed, and the change is not declared as a completion.
3) gradient_rules: "The cost, the plan and the offset are forward-only" and "no gradient reaches them: they stay at their quantile initialisation". This deletes the idea path p_i = one_hot + P - stop_grad(P), through which the reconstruction gradient reaches a_k via |rho_i - s_k| and the encoder via d_c. The idea only allows the quantile-init fallback CONDITIONALLY ("if the baseline detaches P").
4) a_k status is internally contradictory: "parameters": trainable; "inputs": "the fixed code stratum"; "excluded": "the stratum is fixed"; gradient_rules: permanent no-gradient.
5) BEHAVIOUR_OFF justification "the offset is k-independent in that arm (it is the same at every codeword)" is false: the offset is beta*R_c*(1-|rho_i - s_k|), which varies with k through s_k. (What is true is only that a row-constant offset is absorbed by Sinkhorn row scaling; that is not the mechanism offset.)
6) GEOMETRY_OFF says "the offset keeps the same scale R_c = s/rho" - an undefined expression; at c=0 the ball radius 1/sqrt(c) diverges, so R_c must be the frozen constant 1.
7) GEOMETRY_OFF says the arms "differ in the geometry and in nothing else", but beta is re-measured at epoch 0 under the arm metric, so the Euclidean arm has a different beta.
8) "balanced assignment" hard-codes tau = 1 while the idea says the baseline tau.
Evidence: the specification text quoted above. Reasoning: 1-2 change the numbers the mechanism reads, 3-4 change what is trained and contradict the idea coupling, 5-7 make the switches not do what they claim.

computations.definition: From the TRAINING split only: the undirected co-occurrence count matrix A, A_ij = the number of times i and j are adjacent in a training sequence, i != j (self-adjacencies are dropped, so the diagonal is 0). deg_i = the number of distinct training neighbours of i. N(i) = the D highest-count neighbours of i, D = ceil(mean over ALL n_train training items of deg_i, the items with no training edge counted at degree 0, ties by the smaller item id. sim_ij = |N(i) cap N(j)| / sqrt(deg_i * deg_j), in [0,1]. coh_i = (1/deg_i) * sum over j in N(i) of sim_ij, the idea's formula: the sum runs over the TRUNCATED neighbourhood while the normaliser is the FULL degree, so an item with deg_i > D scores lower than the same overlap would score at deg_i <= D. That is the idea's scaling and the specification keeps it. The consequence is stated rather than smoothed over: coh_i carries an item-dependent factor of order deg_i^(-3/2), so the ranking the mechanism uses orders the items by the idea's statistic AS DEFINED - a mixture of the local closure and the degree - and not by the overlap alone. The rank is what enters the cost, and the magnitude never does. coh_i is in [0,1] and is DEFINED for deg_i > 0 only; an item with no training edge has no neighbourhood, no sim and no cohesion, and the rank computation gives it its value.
inputs: the training split's user sequences (history -> target)
computations.name: cohesion statistic
computations.note: defined for the items with at least one training edge; its scale is the idea's, and the ranking inherits it
computations.output: coh_i in [0,1] for every training item with deg_i > 0; undefined for the items with no training edge

computations.definition: Let P = the training items with deg_j > 0 and n_train = the number of training items. For i in P: rho_i = ( #{j in P : coh_j < coh_i} + 0.5 * #{j in P : coh_j = coh_i and j < i} ) / (|P| - 1). The two counts are the idea's, verbatim: the tie term counts only the tied items with a SMALLER index, so tied items receive DIFFERENT ranks. The DENOMINATOR is |P| - 1: the idea was amended in this round (the amendment is in the round's event log and in the idea's own text, which the reviewers read), because the original denominator mixed two populations: the counts run over the items that have a cohesion while the denominator counts every training item, so the rank's support would be [0, (|P|-1)/(n_train-1)] while the codeword strata s_k = sigmoid(alpha_k) span the whole of (0,1) - the two would be on different scales and the top of the codeword ordering could never be the offset's best match. Dividing by |P| - 1 puts the ranked items on the strata's scale, and the idea's range is amended with it: the smallest item's mid-rank is 0, so the rank's range is [0,1] (the codeword strata, being sigmoids, lie in the open interval). The top end is reached only when the top cohesion is unique: with g items tied at the top, the largest rank is (|P| - 1 - 0.5*(g - 1))/(|P| - 1), which is below 1. The strata s_k = sigmoid(alpha_k) lie strictly inside the unit interval, so an item at the very top or the very bottom of the rank has no stratum exactly at its rank and takes the nearest one - a stated boundary effect, not a gap in the mechanism. An item outside P - one with no training edge - has no cohesion and gets rho_i = 0.5, exactly as the idea states; it takes no part in the counts. (If |P| = 1 the denominator is 0 and every item of P takes rho = 0.5.)
inputs: coh_i for every item with at least one training edge
computations.name: cohesion rank
computations.note: the counts are the idea's; the denominator is a declared repair
computations.output: rho_i in [0,1] for the items with an edge (the top reaches 1 only when the top cohesion is unique), and 0.5 for the items without one

computations.definition: s_k = sigmoid(alpha_k) for k = 0..K1-1, with the trainable parameter alpha_k initialised at its quantile, alpha_k = logit((k + 0.5)/K1) (K1 = 256). The strata are a trainable PARAMETER PER CODEWORD, as the idea defines them. Their INITIALISATION is the quantile order of the cohesion rank, so at the start of training the codewords are ordered by behaviour cohesion; the order is a starting point and not a maintained invariant - nothing in the definition, the gradient rules or the training integration keeps alpha_k increasing, and the mechanism reports the per-code mean cohesion rank as a diagnostic so that the drift is measured rather than assumed. The gradient REACHES them: the idea's straight-through estimator p_i = one_hot(k1_i) + P_i - stop_grad(P_i) keeps P in the differentiable path, P depends on C, C depends on |rho_i - s_k| and s_k = sigmoid(alpha_k), so the reconstruction's gradient trains alpha_k.
inputs: the number of level-1 codewords K1
computations.name: code stratum
computations.note: trainable through P, as the idea's STE requires; the quantile order is the initialisation, not an invariant
computations.output: s_k = sigmoid(alpha_k) in (0,1) for every level-1 codeword

computations.definition: The curvature is FIXED at c = 1 (the idea's value), so the ball radius is R_c = 1/sqrt(c) = 1 and the cost is expressed in ball units. LIFT(v) = tanh(sqrt(c)||v||) v / (sqrt(c)||v|| + eps) with eps = 1e-12 and LIFT(0) = 0; MOBIUS substitutes X = -x, so the 2c<.,.> terms are NEGATED: (-x)(+)y = ((1 - 2c<x,y> + c||y||^2)(-x) + (1 - c||x||^2)y) / (1 - 2c<x,y> + c^2||x||^2||y||^2 + eps); DIST(x,y) = (2/sqrt(c)) artanh(min(sqrt(c)||(-x)(+)y||, 1 - 1e-6)). At c = 0 the lift is the identity and DIST(x,y) = 2||x - y||. The sign is the one the reviewers caught in the formula agent's draft: with +2c<.,.> the surface returns 0 at y = -x and its c -> 0 limit is 2||x + y||.
computations.domain: c = 1 for the curved arm; both arguments are lifted, so c||x||^2 < 1 and c||y||^2 < 1, which is where MOBIUS is defined; at c = 0 the model is the Euclidean one and DIST(x,y) = 2||x - y||
computations.name: distance
computations.note: the 2c<.,.> terms are negated because the distance substitutes X = -x into the ball sum: the negated form is the one with d_c(x, x) = 0 and the c -> 0 limit 2||x - y||
computations.output: D_ik (B, K1), the distance of every item to every level-1 codeword

computations.definition: O_ik = beta * R_c * (1 - |rho_i - s_k|) with R_c = 1, in [0, beta]; C_ik = D_k - O_ik. beta = m / R_c with m = the MEDIAN of D_{i,k1(i)} - the distance to the codeword the assignment CHOSE - over the POOLED step-0 batch: every rank contributes the 1023 distances of its own first batch, the ranks all-gather them once, and the median is taken over the pooled 4092 distances, so m is a single global quantile and not a mean of medians. It is measured in a pass with O = 0 (the idea's beta = 0 pass), divided by R_c = 1, and FROZEN. beta is measured ONCE, in the curved configuration (c = 1), and the frozen value is CARRIED into the c = 0 arm, so the two arms differ in the distance and in nothing else. The population is stated because the ranks have different batches: the pooled batch is the union of the four ranks' first batches, so no rank's batch stands for the others'. The offset's scale is therefore the measured level-1 distance scale: no constant is tuned.
computations.name: cost matrix
computations.note: the geodesic term and the behaviour term meet in ONE entry

computations.definition: The mechanism's cost is fed to the BASELINE's Sinkhorn unchanged: the baseline's sinkhorn takes a distance-like matrix and exponentiates it itself, Ktilde_ik = exp(-C_ik / epsilon), with epsilon = its own sk_epsilon and its own sk_iters iterations, and it targets the same marginals as the baseline: row sums 1 per item and column sums B/K1 per codeword (the idea's 'row_sum=1, col_sum=B/K'). The idea writes Ktilde = exp(-C/tau) with tau = the baseline's temperature: that IS the baseline's internal exponentiation step, so the cost is exponentiated ONCE - the specification hands C to the baseline's sinkhorn and does not exponentiate it again. Nothing is centred, nothing is rescaled and no constant is introduced: the mechanism only changes the cost that the baseline's balanced assignment balances. P = Sinkhorn(C, sk_epsilon, sk_iters); k1 = argmax_k P_ik, ties to the smallest k - the baseline's rule (its _indices).
computations.name: balanced assignment
computations.note: the cost goes into the baseline's sinkhorn, once
computations.output: P_ik (B, K1), the transport plan; k1 (B,)

computations.definition: The idea's straight-through estimator through the PLAN: p_i = one_hot(k1_i) + P_i - stop_grad(P_i), so the forward value of the quantised level-1 vector is e1 = sum_k p_ik a_k = a_{k1} exactly, while the gradient flows through the P term into the stratum parameters (through C and |rho_i - s_k|), into the codewords and into the encoder (through d_c). r_next = r - q_i, whose forward value is r - a_{k1}. The reconstruction uses q_i at the baseline position, the commitment term and the optimiser are the baseline's. There is NO deviation from the framework's canonical straight-through: the estimator above IS x_q = x + (x_q - x).detach() with x = P, the plan, and x_q = one_hot(k1). The gradient reaches alpha_k through P precisely because the plan is kept differentiable, which this specification requires; The lifted codebook is written q_lift in the executable listing, because q_k is the RAW codeword the idea uses for the reconstruction and the residual recursion; the forward value of e1 is exactly that raw codeword.
computations.name: level-1 reconstruction and residual
computations.note: the plan is differentiable in the STE: it is the gradient path
computations.output: the reconstruction of level 1 and r_next

computations.definition: loss = baseline_recon + baseline_commit, unchanged. The mechanism has no term of its own: it changes which codeword the balanced assignment picks, and the baseline objective then trains a different quantisation.
inputs: the baseline reconstruction and commitment terms
computations.name: objective
computations.note: no auxiliary loss, no new optimiser
computations.output: the scalar loss the baseline optimiser minimises

executable_statements: eps = 1e-12
def _norm(v): return torch.sqrt(torch.clamp((v * v).sum(-1), min=0.0))
R_c = 1.0                              # FROZEN: the c = 1 ball radius, never recomputed
def lift(v, c): return v if c == 0.0 else v * (torch.tanh(math.sqrt(c) * _norm(v)) / (math.sqrt(c) * _norm(v) + eps)).unsqueeze(-1)

def mobius(x, y, c): return ((1 + 2 * c * (x * y).sum(-1, keepdim=True) + c * (y * y).sum(-1, keepdim=True)) * x + (1 - c * (x * x).sum(-1, keepdim=True)) * y) / (1 + 2 * c * (x * y).sum(-1, keepdim=True) + c * c * (x * x).sum(-1, keepdim=True) * (y * y).sum(-1, keepdim=True) + eps)
def dist(x, y, c): return 2.0 * _norm(x - y) if c == 0.0 else (2.0 / math.sqrt(c)) * torch.atanh(torch.clamp(math.sqrt(c) * _norm(mobius(-x, y, c)), max=1.0 - 1e-6))
s_k = torch.sigmoid(alpha_k)                                 # the trainable code stratum
u = lift(r, c)
q_lift = lift(a, c)
D_k = dist(u[:, None, :], q_lift[None, :, :], c)
O_ik = beta * R_c * (1.0 - torch.abs(rho_i[:, None] - s_k[None, :]))   # the behaviour offset, in [0, beta*R_c]
C_ik = D_k - O_ik
P_ik = sinkhorn(C_ik, sk_epsilon, sk_iters)   # the baseline's plan: it exponentiates C itself
k1 = torch.argmax(P_ik, dim=-1)
p_i = torch.nn.functional.one_hot(k1, K1).float()
p_i = p_i + P_ik - P_ik.detach()            # the idea's STE through the plan
e1 = p_i @ a                               # forward value: a[k1] exactly
r_next = r - e1

spec.mechanism: The level-1 codewords START ordered by a train-only behaviour cohesion rank: each codeword's stratum is initialised at the quantile of the behaviour rank, and the strata are then trained like any other parameter. Each item gets a bounded cohesion rank rho_i in [0,1] from the training split's undirected co-occurrence graph (how tightly its neighbourhood closes into triangles, mid-ranked). Each level-1 codeword k has a stratum s_k = sigmoid(alpha_k) with a trainable alpha_k, initialised at its quantile alpha_k = logit((k + 0.5)/K). The level-1 cost of an item at a codeword is the Poincare distance minus a bounded offset beta*R_c*(1 - |rho_i - s_k|), so an item is cheaper at the codewords whose stratum is close to its own rank. The codeword is chosen by the BASELINE's balanced assignment (a Sinkhorn plan over the cost matrix, then the plan's argmax), never by a plain argmin over the cost: removing the balancing is what collapsed the codebook in round_20261105_144909_130 (42 of 256 level-1 codes, L3 collision 0.703). Levels 2 and 3, the residual recursion, the reconstruction and the loss are the baseline's, unchanged, and the reconstruction uses the UNLIFTED codeword; the mechanism changes TWO things at level 1, and both are declared in the computations: (1) the COST the baseline's balanced assignment balances - the geodesic distance minus the behaviour offset; (2) the PARAMETERS of that cost - the trainable stratum scalars alpha_k. The ESTIMATOR is the framework's canonical straight-through, applied to the plan the balanced assignment produces: x_q = P + (one_hot(k1) - P).detach(). Its forward value is the hard codeword, exactly as the baseline's, and its gradient path runs through the plan - which is a consequence of the plan being differentiable, not a third change. The levels, the residual recursion, the reconstruction, the loss and the optimiser are the baseline's.

objective:
Discover new mechanisms in which TRAINING-ONLY user behaviour and HYPERBOLIC geometry are computationally coupled to improve the RQ-VAE Semantic IDs used by a generative next-item recommender, with the real target of Stage3 test Recall@10 above 0.065.

本轮只做一个**机制**:用**行为图的局部曲率(凝聚度)**指导 SID 的**前缀分组**,同时**保留基线的 Sinkhorn 均衡分配**。目标是让 SID 的层级结构按行为曲率同质:曲率相近的商品更倾向共享较粗的前缀,曲率相差大的商品更倾向分开。

(0) **几何约定**一律按框架契约 tools/research/contracts/HYPERBOLIC_GEOMETRY_CONTRACT.md(球曲率 kappa=-c, c>0, 球半径 R_c=1/sqrt(c); d_c(x,y)=(2/sqrt(c))*artanh(sqrt(c)||(-x)(+)y||); exp_0^c(v)=tanh(sqrt(c)||v||)*v/(sqrt(c)||v||); 切向量的欧氏坐标范数不是黎曼范数(||v||_{0,c}=2||v||))。

(1) **行为侧(只用训练集)**:从训练集的交互序列构造**无向**共现图;每个商品 i 的凝聚度 coh(i) 由其关联边上的三角数(共享邻居数)给出,**必须是有界或秩化的统计**(例如每条关联边的 log1p(三角数) 的均值,或商品在其邻域中的曲率秩)。理由:原始三角数的均值约 700、中位数只有 6,不归一化会让少数 hub 商品主导整个项。coh(i) 只用训练集,不读任何验证/测试交互。

(2) **耦合(必须真实)**:第一层的**均衡分配保留**——Sinkhorn 的代价矩阵带上双曲距离与行为项(C_k = d_c(u_i, q_k) - 偏移),k1 仍由基线的均衡分配给出,**不得**改成普通 argmin(CLAUDE.md 规则 19h:上一轮把一级分配写成 argmin,一级码本坍缩到 42/256,L3 碰撞率 0.703,Stage3 未启动)。行为曲率与双曲几何必须在**同一条计算通路上**相遇:去掉任一侧,都会改变 k1 或损失的值。

(3) **机制的核心项**:一个**排序/对比**项,要求**曲率相近**的商品在同一层共享码字、曲率相差大的商品不共享(即前缀分组按行为曲率同质)。请给出可微表达式(作用在第一层的软分配上,例如按曲率差加权的分配行一致项),并说明:(a) 它与第一层分配/损失的唯一通路是什么;(b) 权重如何由**实测尺度**推出(相对尺度的界或有据可依的默认值),不允许扫参。

(4) **损失** = 基线重构 + commitment + 上述项;STE、层级数(3)、维度、码本大小、优化器、epoch、batch、种子全部不变。重建与残差递推使用**未提升**的码字。

(5) **两个开关必须存在且正确**(代码里存在即可,本轮不训练关闭开关的臂):behaviour off => 曲率项关闭(保留双曲代价与均衡分配);geometry off => c=0(欧氏代价),曲率项仍在。geometry off 就是**同容量欧氏对照**,它必须作为**独立的对照臂**在同族另开一轮(不是本轮的消融),机制臂的报告里要给出对照臂的目录与同一组分层数字。

(6) **预算**:一次正式训练(Stage2 3000 epoch 四卡 + 冻结的 Stage3 协议),不消融训练、不扫参、不多种子、不早停。

(7) 必须给出**可独立复现的公式签名**,并写明 dimensions / gradient_rules(含 STE 与 argmin 的处理)/ training_integration / conventions。

(8) **报告**:分层指标(L1 hard ER、L2 前缀数、L3 碰撞率、L3 refinement gain)与 Stage3 test_R@10;并报告前缀分组的行为曲率同质度(曲率相近的商品共享 L1 的比例,对照随机配对),以便判断机制是否真的起了作用。

papers.title: HVQ-VAE: Variational auto-encoder with hyperbolic vector quantization

papers.abstract: The success of models operating on tokenized data has heightened the need for effective tokenization methods, particularly in vision and auditory tasks where inputs are naturally continuous. A common solution is to employ Vector Quantization (VQ) within VQ Variational Autoencoders (VQVAEs), transforming inputs into discrete tokens by clustering embeddings in Euclidean space. However, Euclidean embeddings not only suffer from inefficient packing and limited separation - due to their polynomial volume growth - but are also prone to codebook collapse, where only a small subset of codebook vectors are effectively utilized. To address these limitations, we introduce HyperVQ, a novel approach that formulates VQ as a hyperbolic Multinomial Logistic Regression (MLR) problem, leveraging the exponential volume growth in hyperbolic space to mitigate collapse and improve cluster separability. Additionally, HyperVQ represents codebook vectors as geometric representatives of hyperbolic decision hyperplanes, encouraging disentangled and robust latent representations. Our experiments demonstrate that HyperVQ matches traditional VQ in generative and reconstruction tasks, while surpassing it in disc
papers.title: HyperVQ: MLR-based Vector Quantization in Hyperbolic Space

papers.abstract:
Abstract: Based on the formal equivalence between the non-relativistic Schrödinger equation and the relativistic Klein-Gordon equation and using the proper quantization rule as well as the Riccati equation solution, exact solutions are established for a set of interaction potentials (second Rosen-Morse, Pöschl-Teller, second Pöschl-Teller, Scarf II, and Eckart hyperbolic type potentials). The calculations are elaborated in the case of equal scalar and vector potentials. The general case of unequal scalar-vector potentials is detailed for the case of harmonic potential class.
Keywords: Proper quantization rule, Exact solutions, Klein-Gordon equation, Riccati equation.
PACS number: 03.65.Ge; 03.65.Fd; 03.65.Bz; 03.65.−w.
papers.title: A Proper Quantization Rule for Solving the Klein-Gordon Equation with Equal and Unequal Scalar and Vector Interaction Potentials

papers.abstract: In this paper, two semi-supervised appearance based loop closure detection technique, HGCN-FABMAP and HGCN-BoW are introduced. Furthermore an extension to the current state of the art localization SLAM algorithm, ORB-SLAM, is presented. The proposed HGCN-FABMAP method is implemented in an off-line manner incorporating Bayesian probabilistic schema for loop detection decision making. Specifically, we let a Hyperbolic Graph Convolutional Neural Network (HGCN) to operate over the SURF features graph space, and perform vector quantization part of the SLAM procedure. This part previously was performed in an unsupervised manner using algorithms like HKmeans, kmeans++,..etc. The main Advantage of using HGCN, is that it scales linearly in number of graph edges. Experimental results shows that HGCN-FABMAP algorithm needs far more cluster centroids than HGCN-ORB, otherwise it fails to detect loop closures. Therefore we consider HGCN-ORB to be more efficient in terms of memory consumption, also we conclude the superiority of HGCN-BoW and HGCN-FABMAP with respect to other algorithms.
papers.title: Semi-supervised Vector-Quantization in Visual SLAM using HGCN

papers.abstract: Nonlinearity is crucial to the performance of a deep (neural) network (DN). To date there has been little progress understanding the menagerie of available nonlinearities, but recently progress has been made on understanding the r\^ole played by piecewise affine and convex nonlinearities like the ReLU and absolute value activation functions and max-pooling. In particular, DN layers constructed from these operations can be interpreted as {\em max-affine spline operators} (MASOs) that have an elegant link to vector quantization (VQ) and $K$-means. While this is good theoretical progress, the entire MASO approach is predicated on the requirement that the nonlinearities be piecewise affine and convex, which precludes important activation functions like the sigmoid, hyperbolic tangent, and softmax. {\em This paper extends the MASO framework to these and an infinitely large class of new nonlinearities by linking deterministic MASOs with probabilistic Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs).} We show that, under a GMM, piecewise affine, convex nonlinearities like ReLU, absolute value, and max-pooling can be interpreted as solutions to certain natural "hard" VQ inference problems, while sigmoid, hy

papers.abstract: We theoretically study the infrared reflectivity and transmissivity of a high-temperature layered superconductor slab. Both infrared spectra exhibit very narrow Fabry–Perot resonances associated with the quantization of the wave vector of the TM electromagnetic modes. The resonances are observed in a pass band where the refractive index of the layered superconductor is negative. The pass band of negative dispersion is above the Josephson plasma frequency which appears in the expression for the effective permittivity component, corresponding to the direction perpendicular to the layers. It was found that the Fabry–Perot resonances undergo a blue shift as the slab thickness or the angle of incidence are increased. papers.abstract: The proposed algorithm in this paper is the quantized minimum kernel risk hyperbolic secant adaptive filtering algorithm, which offers a simplified approach to enhancing the performance and stability of kernel adaptive filtering in non-Gaussian noise environments. The algorithm features a newly developed minimum kernel risk hyperbolic secant cost function, which harnesses the hyperbolic secant function’s strengths to diminish outlier impacts and expedite convergence. In addition, its convex kernel risk-sensitive loss surface facilitates swift and accurate filtering via gradient-based methods, thus ensuring outlier robustness. This method could effectively manage network size and reduce computational complexity by incorporating vector quantization for inputting spatial data. Simulation tests in Mackey–Glass time series prediction and nonlinear system identification have indicated that the minimum kernel hyperbolic secant adaptive filtering algorithm and its quantized variant excel in terms of convergence speed, robustness, and computational efficiency.

papers.abstract: We present hyperbolix, an open-source library for hyperbolic deep learning in JAX, built on Flax NNX. To our knowledge, it is the first comprehensive, general-purpose hyperbolic deep learning library in JAX. It includes six manifolds with a common interface: Euclidean space, the Poincar\'e ball, the hyperboloid, the $\kappa$-stereographic model, mixed-curvature product spaces, and the proper velocity space. We implement layer families that cover linear layers, convolutions, attention, normalization, positional encoding, regression, and vector quantization. These building blocks span methods ranging from Ganea's original hyperbolic neural networks to recent fully hyperbolic architectures such as Hypformer and Lorentzian ResNet. Additionally, hyperbolix contains Riemannian optimizers implemented as optax transformations, wrapped distributions, and hyperbolic dimensionality-reduction techniques. Its API uses idiomatic JAX: Manifolds are stateless, with curvature being passed at call time, while manifold operations act on single points, with vmap enabling batch operations. papers.abstract: Singular interactions can reshape quantum spectra by changing admissible wavefunction domains. papers.abstract: The goal of quantization is to find the best approximation of a probability distribution by a discrete measure with finite support. When dealing with empirical distributions, this boils down to finding the best summary of the data by a smaller number of points, and automatically yields a k-means-type clustering. In this paper, we introduce Competitive Learning Riemannian Quantization (CLRQ), an online quantization algorithm that applies when the data does not belong to a vector space, but rather a Riemannian manifold. It can be seen as a density approximation procedure as well as a clustering method. papers.abstract: The success of models operating on tokenized data has heightened the need for effective tokenization methods, particularly in vision and auditory tasks where inputs are naturally continuous. A common solution is to employ Vector Quantization (VQ) within VQ Variational Autoencoders (VQVAEs), transforming inputs into discrete tokens by clustering embeddings in Euclidean space. However, Euclidean embeddings not only suffer from inefficient packing and limited separation - due to their polynomial volume growth - but are also prone to codebook collapse, where only a small subset of codebook vectors are effectively utilized. To address these limitations, we introduce HyperVQ, a novel approach that formulates VQ as a hyperbolic Multinomial Logistic Regression (MLR) problem, leveraging the exponential volume growth in hyperbolic space to mitigate collapse and improve cluster separability. Additionally, HyperVQ represents codebook vectors as geometric representatives of hyperbolic decision hyperplanes, encouraging disentangled and robust latent representations. papers.abstract: We present a novel vector quantization (VQ) module for the two state-of-the-art long-range simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) algorithms. For the first time, we have considered the space formed by these SURF features, robust image descriptors, as a graph, enabling us to apply an HGCN in the VQ section which results in an improved LCD performance. papers.abstract: Vector Quantized Variational AutoEncoders (VQ-VAEs) are designed to compress a continuous input to a discrete latent space and reconstruct it with minimal distortion. They operate by maintaining a set of vectors -- often referred to as the codebook -- and quantizing each encoder output to the nearest vector in the codebook. However, as vector quantization is non-differentiable, the gradient to the encoder flows around the vector quantization layer rather than through it in a straight-through approximation. This approximation may be undesirable as all information from the vector quantization operation is lost. In this work, we propose a way to propagate gradients through the vector quantization layer of VQ-VAEs. We smoothly transform each encoder output into its corresponding codebook vector via a rotation and rescaling linear transformation that is treated as a constant during backpropagation. As a result, the relative magnitude and angle between encoder output and codebook vector becomes encoded into the gradient as it propagates through the vector quantization layer and back to the encoder. Across 11 different VQ-VAE training paradigms, we find this restructuring improves reconst

papers.abstract: Most high-performance block-coding systems for image compression, such as JPEG, have been designed for software or dedicated digital hardware implementations where the data are already assumed to be available in digital format. In modern CMOS photosensors, smart-pixel technologies have allowed the realization of basic signal processing tasks at the pixel level, in analog format before analog-to-digital (A/D) conversion. The elimination of A/D converters and implementation of block-coding directly over analog blocks of pixels in such sensors can be attractive both in terms of area savings and power consumption. The design of block encoders, under the strong hardware constraints that derive from the A/D converter removal, has been investigated in this paper. We present a comparison of three systems in terms of rate, distortion and complexity, and present a numerical simulation analysis of their sensitivity to implementation errors. The conclusion of the analysis is that linear-transform coding vector quantizers outperform full-search vector quantizers and warping hyperbolic-tangent neural networks, in terms of performance, complexity and robustness, for a CMOS imaging sensor implemen
papers.title: Sensitivity analysis of low-complexity vector quantizers for focal-plane image compression

papers.abstract: Vector quantization is a technique in machine learning that discretizes continuous representations into a set of discrete vectors. It is widely employed in tokenizing data representations for large language models, diffusion models, and other generative models. Despite its prevalence, the characteristics and behaviors of vector quantization in generative models remain largely underexplored. In this study, we investigate representation collapse in vector quantization - a critical degradation where codebook tokens or latent embeddings lose their discriminative power by converging to a limited subset of values. This collapse fundamentally compromises the model's ability to capture diverse data patterns. By leveraging both synthetic and real datasets, we identify the severity of each type of collapses and triggering conditions. Our analysis reveals that restricted initialization and limited encoder capacity result in tokens collapse and embeddings collapse. Building on these findings, we propose potential solutions aimed at mitigating each collapse. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive study examining representation collapsing problems in vector quantization.
papers.title: Representation Collapsing Problems in Vector Quantization

papers.abstract: Graph embedding based retrieval has become one of the most popular techniques in the information retrieval community and search engine industry. The classical paradigm mainly relies on the flat Euclidean geometry. In recent years, hyperbolic (negative curvature) and spherical (positive curvature) representation methods have shown their superiority to capture hierarchical and cyclic data structures respectively. However, in industrial scenarios such as e-commerce sponsored search platforms, the large-scale heterogeneous query-item-advertisement interaction graphs often have multiple structures coexisting. Existing methods either only consider a single geometry space, or combine several spaces manually, which are incapable and inflexible to model the complexity and heterogeneity in the real scenario. papers.abstract: Semantic IDs represent items as shared discrete token sequences and have become a practical tool for recommendation and retrieval. Yet it remains difficult to tell why a tokenizer fails: poor quality may come from codebook underutilization, unstable decision boundaries, or geometric distortion of the embedding space. This paper develops a quantitative framework for diagnosing these failures through expected codeword overlap and effective codebook capacity. The former measures expected codeword confusion under retrieval-time perturbation, while the latter converts that confusion into an effective number of usable, well-separated codes. The framework links semantic boundary confusion to both code usage imbalance and Euclidean geometric constraints. As a proof of concept, we present Decoupled Residual Quantization (DRQ), which separates continuous geometry reconstruction from discrete distribution matching. Experiments on a large-scale industrial dataset show that Semantic ID quality is multi-objective: symbolic robustness, reconstruction fidelity, and behavior-aware soft matching each stress different aspects of a tokenizer. papers.title: Decoupled Residual Quantization for Robust Semantic IDs in Recommendation

papers.abstract: Our languages are in constant flux driven by external factors such as cultural, societal and technological changes, as well as by only partially understood internal motivations. Words acquire new meanings and lose old senses, new words are coined or borrowed from other languages and obsolete words slide into obscurity. Understanding the characteristics of shifts in the meaning and in the use of words is useful for those who work with the content of historical texts, the interested general public, but also in and of itself. The findings from automatic lexical semantic change detection, and the models of diachronic conceptual change are currently being incorporated in approaches for measuring document across-time similarity, information retrieval from long-term document archives, the design of OCR algorithms, and so on. In recent years we have seen a surge in interest in the academic community in computational methods and tools supporting inquiry into diachronic conceptual change and lexical replacement. This article is an extract of a survey of recent computational techniques to tackle lexical semantic change currently under review. In this article we focus on diachronic conceptual

papers.abstract: Novelty alone is not sufficient for innovation. For new ideas and products to thrive, they must find their place within the existing societal fabric, such as institutions, conventions, and infrastructures that have been built over time. Past successes create inertia, favoring conservative advances. Here, we develop a quantitative framework to map the contours of the adjacent possible in the presence of the power of typicality. Typical assemblies, frequently combined building blocks in past innovations, compress and curve the space of possibilities toward what is imaginable, accessible, and implementable, much like gravitational forces on new ideas and actions. We demonstrate that these curvatures in the space of possibilities are not just abstract constructs but empirically measurable through two complementary studies. We first show that Edison's inventions are primarily located in areas of high curvature, aligning with his strategy of building upon institutionalized domains. In contrast, Tesla's inventions are mainly found in low-curvature areas, indicating his propensity for exploring new territories and pushing innovation boundaries. papers.abstract: Mixed-curvature representation learning seeks to capture rich geometric structures that cannot be adequately modeled by a single curvature regime. Existing approaches largely rely on product manifolds, which require manually specifying how different curvature spaces are combined and separate their curvature contributions across factors. We introduce the $\mathbb{SL}(n)$ space, a representation geometry defined by the simple $\det(A)=1$ constraint and a left invariant Schatten-$p$ Finsler structure. Despite this minimal construction, $\mathbb{SL}(n)$ exhibits pointwise negative, zero, and positive flag curvature around a common flagpole, while its mixed-curvature and curvature-coupling capacities are asymptotically maximal relative to the intrinsic geometric upper bound. Beyond geometry, its noncommutative group structure provides inherent order sensitivity, and its non-nilpotent Lie algebra admits nonzero nested Lie brackets at arbitrary depth, enabling deep order-aware composition. Empirically, $\mathbb{SL}(n)$ consistently outperforms a broad range of representation manifold baselines across graph benchmarks at different scales. It reduces average distortion over the strongest ba
papers.title: $\mathbb{SL}(n)$ Representation Learning: An Intrinsic Mixed-Curvature Space with Higher Curvature Capacities and Deeper Order-Aware Composition

papers.abstract: Recently, deformable convolution networks have shown the superior performance in object detection due to its ability to adapt to the geometric variations of object. These methods learn the offset fields under the supervision of localization and recognition. Nevertheless, the spatial support of these networks may be inexact because the offsets are learned implicitly via extra convolutional layer. In this work, we present curvature-driven deformable convolutional networks (C-DCNets) that adopt explicit geometric property of the preceding feature maps to enhance the deformability of convolution operation and make the networks easier to focus on pertinent image region. To be consistent with postprocessing technology of object detection, we multiply the class prediction probability by the similarity of predicted boxes and ground truth boxes as the final class prediction probability and substitute it into the binary cross entropy loss function. The obtained loss function correlates the bounding box regression and classification. Experimental results on PASCAL VOC and COCO data set show that C-DCNets-based YOLOv4 with the proposed loss function outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms.
papers.title: Curvature-Driven Deformable Convolutional Networks for End-To-End Object Detection

papers.abstract: Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is a cornerstone of modern text-to-image models, yet its reliance on a semantically vacuous null prompt ($\varnothing$) generates a guidance signal prone to geometric entanglement. This is a key factor limiting its precision, leading to well-documented failures in complex compositional tasks. We propose Condition-Degradation Guidance (CDG), a novel paradigm that replaces the null prompt with a strategically degraded condition, $\boldsymbol{c}_{\text{deg}}$. This reframes guidance from a coarse "good vs. null" contrast to a more refined "good vs. almost good" discrimination, thereby compelling the model to capture fine-grained semantic distinctions. We find that tokens in transformer text encoders split into two functional roles: content tokens encoding object semantics, and context-aggregating tokens capturing global context. By selectively degrading only the former, CDG constructs $\boldsymbol{c}_{\text{deg}}$ without external models or training. Validated across diverse architectures including Stable Diffusion 3, FLUX, and Qwen-Image, CDG markedly improves compositional accuracy and text-image alignment. As a lightweight, plug-and-play module, it ac
papers.title: Guiding Diffusion Models with Semantically Degraded Conditions

papers.abstract: Several first order stochastic optimization methods commonly used in the Euclidean domain such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD), accelerated gradient descent or variance reduced methods have already been adapted to certain Riemannian settings. However, some of the most popular of these optimization tools - namely Adam , Adagrad and the more recent Amsgrad - remain to be generalized to Riemannian manifolds. We discuss the difficulty of generalizing such adaptive schemes to the most agnostic Riemannian setting, and then provide algorithms and convergence proofs for geodesically convex objectives in the particular case of a product of Riemannian manifolds, in which adaptivity is implemented across manifolds in the cartesian product. Our generalization is tight in the sense that choosing the Euclidean space as Riemannian manifold yields the same algorithms and regret bounds as those that were already known for the standard algorithms. Experimentally, we show faster convergence and to a lower train loss value for Riemannian adaptive methods over their corresponding baselines on the realistic task of embedding the WordNet taxonomy in the Poincare ball.
papers.title: Riemannian Adaptive Optimization Methods

papers.abstract: Recommender systems have become an essential component of many online platforms, providing personalized recommendations to users. A crucial aspect is embedding techniques that convert the high-dimensional discrete features, such as user and item IDs, into low-dimensional continuous vectors, which can enhance the recommendation performance. Embedding techniques have revolutionized the capture of complex entity relationships, generating significant research interest. This survey presents a comprehensive analysis of recent advances in recommender system embedding techniques. We examine centralized embedding approaches across matrix, sequential, and graph structures. In matrix-based scenarios, collaborative filtering generates embeddings that effectively model user-item preferences, particularly in sparse data environments. For sequential data, we explore various approaches including recurrent neural networks and self-supervised methods such as contrastive and generative learning. In graph-structured contexts, we analyze techniques like node2vec that leverage network relationships, along with applicable self-supervised methods. papers.title: Embedding in Recommender Systems: A Survey

papers.abstract: A growing number of applications require dictionaries of words belonging to semantic classes present in specialized domains. Manually constructed knowledge bases often do not provide sufficient coverage of specialized vocabulary and require substantial effort to build and keep up-to-date. In this thesis, we propose a semi-supervised approach to the construction of domain-specific semantic lexicons based on the distributional similarity hypothesis. Our method starts with a small set of seed words representing the target class and an unannotated text corpus. It locates instances of seed words in the text and generates lexical patterns from their contexts; these patterns in turn extract more words/phrases that belong to the semantic category in an iterative manner. This bootstrapping process can be continued until the output lexicon reaches the desired size. \nWe explore employing techniques such as learning lexicons for multiple semantic classes at the same time and using feedback from competing lexicons to increase the learning precision. papers.title: A Semi-Supervised Approach to the Construction of Semantic Lexicons

papers.abstract: Recently, graph-aware Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promising capabilities in jointly modeling graph-structured data and textual information. Existing approaches typically employ a graph encoder and a frozen LLM to obtain node representations from graph and textual views, followed by node-level alignment to bridge the two modalities. However, such alignment mechanisms primarily focus on node information while overlooking edge-level structures, leading to suboptimal information propagation across views. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive theoretical analysis to uncover why node-level alignment is insufficient for aligning textual and graph representations. Specifically, we prove theoretically for the first time that neglecting edge information leads to suboptimal solutions and negatively curved edges induce bottlenecked information flow, giving rise to the over-squashing phenomenon between graph and textual views. papers.title: Edge-Aware Curvature Modeling for Graph Understanding in Large Language Models

papers.abstract: The localization of peripheral proteins to specific sites of cell membranes is a pivotal step in many cellular processes. Many such processes involve dynamic changes in membrane structure and particularly membrane curvature. Although certain proteins have been implicated in these processes, many questions remain as to the mechanisms underlying their involvement. A major goal toward this end is to elucidate mechanisms by which they generate and sense membrane curvature. The membrane curvature sensing and generation properties of the peripherally binding endocytic accessory protein endophilin are believed to depend on its dimeric structure. We therefore first study endophilin dimerization kinetics and equilibria in solution, employing Förster resonance energy transfer techniques. Mechanistic insights into the association of endophilin N-BAR with membranes are obtained from kinetic studies by stopped-flow rapid mixing techniques. papers.abstract: The mouse is a pervasive input device used for a wide range of interactive applications. However, computational modelling of mouse behaviour typically requires time-consuming design and extraction of handcrafted features, or approaches that are application-specific. We instead propose Mouse2Vec – a novel self-supervised method designed to learn semantic representations of mouse behaviour that are reusable across users and applications. Mouse2Vec uses a Transformer-based encoder-decoder architecture, which is specifically geared for mouse data: During pretraining, the encoder learns an embedding of input mouse trajectories while the decoder reconstructs the input and simultaneously detects mouse click events. We show that the representations learned by our method can identify interpretable mouse behaviour clusters and retrieve similar mouse trajectories. We also demonstrate on three sample downstream tasks that the representations can be practically used to augment mouse data for training supervised methods and serve as an effective feature extractor.
papers.title: Mouse2Vec: Learning Reusable Semantic Representations of Mouse Behaviour

papers.abstract: People have complex thoughts, and they often express their thoughts with complex sentences using natural languages. This complexity may facilitate efficient communications among the audience with the same knowledge base. But on the other hand, for a different or new audience this composition becomes cumbersome to understand and analyze. Analysis of such compositions using syntactic or semantic measures is a challenging job and defines the base step for natural language processing. In this dissertation I explore and propose a number of new techniques to analyze and visualize the syntactic and semantic patterns of unstructured English texts. The syntactic analysis is done through a proposed visualization technique which categorizes and compares different English compositions based on their different reading complexity metrics. For the semantic analysis I use Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) to analyze the hidden patterns in complex compositions. I have used this technique to analyze comments from a social visualization web site for detecting the irrelevant ones (e.g., spam). The patterns of collaborations are also studied through statistical analysis. Word sense disambiguation is used
papers.title: Syntactic and Semantic Analysis and Visualization of Unstructured English Texts

STEP 1 - scope screening of the five proposals against the frozen bundles.
Read: all five bundles (d69fbb2eeb4c9ab0, 6b5ae2abeecaab25, df96b282930cef5f, bc49cd02b60c2754, 73aab3babfa88c58) plus the shared ledger E18-E25 and the train-only probes E5/E6.
Observed: every proposal keeps the baseline balanced Sinkhorn and takes the hard level index as row-argmax of the balanced plan (cohrank "k_i = argmax_k P_ik"; CURV_COH "row argmax of P as in the baseline code"; curvature-stratum "baseline's argmax over the balanced plan"; hyperbolic_behavior "argmax_k P_ik from this balanced P"; scc-l1 "code(i)=argmax_k P1_ik"). None replaces the balanced assignment with a plain argmin, so the anti-collapse clause is respected by all five and none is OUT_OF_SCOPE on that ground.
Also observed: all five bundles contain the same generic proxy results - E11 geometry_operator_valid PASS, E12 behavior_dependency FAIL, E13 geometry_dependency PASS (1 of top-1 changed), E14 CANDIDATE_PATH_NOT_RUN, E10 only "proposed" Euclidean control - so the bundles do not differentiate the candidates; only the proposal text, the shared probes (E5 graph, E6 prefix statistic) and the shared ledger (E18-E25) can.
Discriminators I will use: (a) faithfulness to the baseline's Sinkhorn marginals/temperature/iterations and to the baseline objective, (b) whether the coupling constant is derived or defaulted, (c) magnitude of the perturbation of the level-1 plan, (d) whether the behaviour partner coordinate is a code radius (the ledger's weakest family) or an in-rho learned stratum, (e) per-step cost.
Open: final ordering and reasons.

STEP 2 - evidence-grounded comparison and ranking decision.
Shared evidence used: E5 measured train graph 118315 edges, mean_outgoing_degree 5.4526 -> sparse, so item-level triangle cohesion is noisy; E6 same_first_prefix_rate 0.0907 vs permuted null 0.067 -> the level-1 prefix carries only a weak behavioural signal, so heavy forcing of behaviour homogeneity at level 1 is risky. Ledger E18-E25 (all comparable_to_frozen=false, global_batch 16384, none at the frozen protocol): best observed 0.05459705 (BRANCH_CONDITIONED_FRECHET_RESIDUAL, E19), 0.05438813 (CURV-RESID-CONTRAST, E24), 0.05165480 (CONCMID-GEO-SID, E22), 0.05000087 (COOC_RANK_FRECHET, E23), 0.04822507 (BEHDIR-L4, E18), and the radius-parameter arm BRad-RQ lowest at 0.04460384 and 0.03060638 (E20/E21). Nothing in the ledger reaches the 0.065 target, so ranking is comparative plausibility.
Decision: (1) CURV_COH_PREFIX_SINKHORN - only candidate whose behaviour offset is capped at 10% of the measured curved-distance scale and confined to level 1, so Sinkhorn and Euclidean levels 2-3 stay verbatim (smallest perturbation of the balanced plan; penalty noted: its a_k is code depth, the BRad-RQ radius family). (2) curvature-stratum-sinkhorn-v1 - cleanest modification (cost matrix only, no second loss), derived beta from the epoch-0 median distance, stratum in rho space not radius, but the tent kernel at median-distance scale risks a hard behaviour-quantile partition on a sparse graph (E5) and can cost the coherence that BEHDIR-L4 (0.0482) lost. (3) cohrank-curvature-sinkhorn-v1 - well specified, derived scales, but median-scale offset at all three levels plus a full-weight curvature-variance loss, ~785k curved entries/step. (4) scc-l1-curvcoherence - renormalises the cost by the batch median (changes effective entropy), behaviour centres from detached running-mean buffers fed by a discarded first Sinkhorn pass. (5) hyperbolic_behavior_curvature_sinkhorn_v1 - couples to a centred code radius with arbitrary sign (the BRad-RQ family), D_med renormalisation plus a 16k-edge contrastive term, lambda=1 default.
Open: none; full answer appended next.
